For it agreed with the sacraments of the law in this, that it was only a sign; and with the sacraments of the new law and of grace in this, that it disposed closely to grace; and in form and matter it had an agreement with our Baptism, for it was given in water in the name of Christ. — It is asked, then, under what form John baptized. The answer is: under this form, “I baptize thee in the name of Him who is to come”, according to the words: [[Acts 19:4|John baptized the people|Joannes baptizabat populum]], [[Acts 19:4|saying: That they should believe in him, who was to come after him, that is to say, in Jesus|dicens, in eum qui venturus esset post ipsum, ut crederent, hoc est in Jesum]]. For although Christ had then come in the flesh, He had not yet come to preach.

paras.t: Sed si baptismus Joannis non præstitit gratiam, quæritur cur baptizavit. Respondendum, quod multas ob causas, quarum primam ipsemet tangit Joannes loquens de Christo: Ut manifestaretur, inquit, in Israel, propterea veni ego in aqua baptizans, id est ad hoc ut ostenderem populo Israel, quod Christus est qui baptizat in Spiritu Sancto. Ex hoc enim quod Joannes baptizavit, quod nulli Prophetarum ante eum concessum est, concurrebat ad eum populus, sicque omnibus manifestare potuit Christum, cujus fuit ipse præcursor. Secundo, ut ordinem suæ præcursionis in omnibus observaret, quatenus sicut Christum prævenit nascendo et prædicando, sic eum quoque præcederet baptizando. Tertio, ut ad Christi Baptismum disponeret: quod enim catechumenis nondum baptizatis confert instructio fidei, hoc contulit credentibus baptismus Joannis. Quarto, ut homines ad pœnitendum induceret. Quinto, ut ad suscipiendum Christi Baptismum homines assuetos efficeret. Quoniam ergo baptismus Joannis dabatur in nomine venturi, videlicet Christi, idcirco erat quædam protestatio atque professio credendi in Christum, et opera pœnitentiæ digna agendi: ordinabatur quippe ad hæc. Et quia pœnitentia non competit pueris, ideo eis non conferebatur, sicut nec feminis, ut aliqui dicunt, quoniam instruendæ erant per viros. Quamvis autem baptismus Joannis non contulit gratiam sua virtute, tamen ex fide et devotione suscipientis, ex sanctitate quoque et precibus dantis, præstitit gratiam, sicut et sacramenta legis.
paras.en: But if the baptism of John did not give grace, it is asked why he baptized. The answer is that he did so for many reasons, the first of which John himself touches on when speaking of Christ. He says: [[John 1:31|that he may be made manifest in Israel, therefore am I come baptizing with water|Ut manifestaretur, inquit, in Israel, propterea veni ego in aqua baptizans]], that is, to this end, that I might show the people of Israel that Christ is He who baptizes in the Holy Ghost. For because John baptized, which had been granted to none of the Prophets before him, the people flocked to him, and so he was able to make Christ known to all, whose forerunner he was. Secondly, that he might keep the order of his forerunning in all things, so that, as he went before Christ in being born and in preaching, so he might also go before Him in baptizing. Thirdly, to dispose men for the Baptism of Christ: for what instruction in the faith gives to catechumens not yet baptized, the baptism of John gave to those who believed. Fourthly, to lead men to do penance. Fifthly, to accustom men to receiving the Baptism of Christ. Since, then, the baptism of John was given in the name of Him who was to come, namely Christ, it was a kind of declaration and profession of believing in Christ and of doing works worthy of penance; for it was ordered to these things. And because penance does not belong to children, it was not given to them; nor to women either, as some say, since they were to be instructed through the men. And although the baptism of John did not confer grace by its own power, yet it did give grace by reason of the faith and devotion of the one receiving it, and of the holiness and prayers of the one giving it, as did the sacraments of the law also.

paras.t: Videns autem Joannes multos Pharisæorum et Sadducæorum venientes ad baptismum suum, dixit eis. In populo Judæorum erant tres sectæ, quæ se ceteris præferebant, puta: Essæi, qui abstractam et rigorosissimam vitam duxerunt, sed erraverunt in multis, putantes se sua justitia sine gratia posse salvari. Pharisæi quoque, qui quasi divisi ab aliis, dicebantur quasi religiosiores et doctiores. Eratque honesta secta eorum: de qua se Paulus fuisse testatur, Ego, inquiens, Pharisæus sum, filius Pharisæorum. Item et Sadducæi, dicentes se natos de semine Sadoc pontificis: qui libros Moysis recipientes, Prophetas non receperunt, et nec angelum, nec spiritum, nec resurrectionem concesserunt, quæ omnia Pharisæi admiserunt.
paras.en: [[3:7|And seeing|Videns autem]] John [[3:7|many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said to them|multos Pharisæorum et Sadducæorum venientes ad baptismum suum, dixit eis]]. Among the Jewish people there were three sects which set themselves above the rest. The Essenes, who led a withdrawn and most rigorous life, but erred in many things, thinking that they could be saved by their own justice without grace. The Pharisees also, who, being as it were set apart from the others [the name was taken to mean “the separated”], were held to be more religious and more learned; and their sect was an honourable one: Paul testifies that he belonged to it, saying: [[Acts 23:6|I am a Pharisee, the son of Pharisees|Pharisæus sum, filius Pharisæorum]]. And likewise the Sadducees, who said that they were born of the seed of Sadoc the high priest; they accepted the books of Moses but did not accept the Prophets, and they admitted neither angel, nor spirit, nor resurrection, all of which the Pharisees admitted.

paras.t: His ergo dixit Joannes: Progenies viperarum, id est, generatio seu filii serpentium, videlicet perversorum venenatorumque patrum, quis demonstravit vobis fugere a ventura ira? Locus iste dupliciter explanatur. Ambrosius enim super Lucam exponit, ut sit commendatio pœnitentium, hoc modo: Genimina, id est, progenies, viperarum, id est patrum impiorum: non tamen impii filii, quoniam pœnitentes. Ad generationem itaque, non ad successionem, id est ad genitores, non ad filios, referenda est comparatio viperarum, secundum Ambrosium. Quis demonstravit vobis, id est, quis docuit vos jam pœnitentes, fugere a ventura ira, id est timere extremum judicium, et vitam corrigere, per quod sententia damnationis vitatur? Nullus utique, nisi misericors Deus, quum sitis filii pessimorum. Facite ergo fructum dignum pœnitentiæ: id est, quia jam datum est vobis intus pœnitere, curate exterius opera satisfactionis idoneæ perpetrare, quatenus secundum mensuram peccati et delectationis illicitæ, sit mensura operum pœnitentialium et afflictionis spontaneæ: juxta illud, Quantum glorificavit se, et in deliciis fuit, tantum date ei luctum et tormentum. Peccata nempe sunt vulnera animæ; medicina vero est pœnitentia. Certum est quod vulnera profundiora ac magis mortifera, majori ac acerbiori indigent medicina.
paras.en: To these, then, John said: [[3:7|Ye brood of vipers|Progenies viperarum]], that is, generation or children of serpents, namely of perverse and venomous fathers, [[3:7|who hath shewed you to flee from the wrath to come|quis demonstravit vobis fugere a ventura ira]]? This place is explained in two ways. Ambrose, on Luke, expounds it as a commendation of the penitent, in this way: [[Luke 3:7|Ye offspring|Genimina]], that is, brood, [[Luke 3:7|of vipers|viperarum]], that is, of wicked fathers; yet not wicked sons, since they are doing penance. And so the comparison with vipers is to be referred to the generation, not to the succession, that is, to the parents, not to the children, according to Ambrose. [[3:7|Who hath shewed you|Quis demonstravit vobis]], that is, who has taught you, already penitent, [[3:7|to flee from the wrath to come|fugere a ventura ira]], that is, to fear the last judgment and to amend your lives, by which the sentence of damnation is avoided? None, surely, but the merciful God, since you are the children of most wicked men. [[3:8|Bring forth therefore fruit worthy of penance|Facite ergo fructum dignum pœnitentiæ]]: that is, since it has now been given you to repent inwardly, take care to perform outwardly works of fitting satisfaction, so that the measure of your penitential works and of the affliction you take on willingly may answer to the measure of the sin and of the unlawful pleasure; according to the words: [[Apoc 18:7|As much as she hath glorified herself and lived in delicacies, so much torment and sorrow give ye to her|Quantum glorificavit se, et in deliciis fuit, tantum date ei luctum et tormentum]]. For sins are wounds of the soul, and penance is the medicine; and it is certain that deeper and more deadly wounds need a greater and sharper medicine.

paras.t: Secundo exponitur secundum Chrysostomum et Bedam, ut sit exprobratio impœnitentium ficte venientium ad baptismum, ut insidientur Joanni. His igitur loquitur: Progenies viperarum, id est, venenati fallacesque filii patrum serpentinorum, quorum venenosam pravitatem ac simulationem sectamini, quis demonstravit vobis fugere a ventura ira? id est, nullus potest vobis dare consilium, viam seu modum evadendi divinæ justitiæ ultionem vobis imminentem, nisi pœniteatis: et quamvis nunc occultetis hominibus vestram malitiam, tamen in die judicii deducetur in publicum. Unde in Sapientia scribitur: Manum tuam, Domine, impossibile est effugere; et in Psalmo, Quo ibo a spiritu tuo, et quo a facie tua fugiam? Facite ergo fructum dignum pœnitentiæ, scilicet ex intimo corde, cum diligenti custodia mentis et animo timorato, ne recidivetis. Horrendum est enim incidere in manus Dei viventis. Porro, quod iste sit sensus, videtur ex eo quod infra habetur, quemadmodum Christo interrogante Pharisæos, Baptismus Joannis de cœlo erat, an ex hominibus? non audebant respondere, De cœlo, scientes quod diceret ipsis: Quare ergo vos non credidistis ei?
paras.en: Secondly, it is expounded according to Chrysostom and Bede as a reproach of the impenitent, who were coming to baptism in pretence, to lay snares for John. To these, then, he says: [[3:7|Ye brood of vipers|Progenies viperarum]], that is, venomous and deceitful sons of serpent fathers, whose poisonous wickedness and pretence you follow, [[3:7|who hath shewed you to flee from the wrath to come|quis demonstravit vobis fugere a ventura ira]]? That is, no one can give you counsel, or a way or means of escaping the vengeance of divine justice that hangs over you, unless you repent; and though you now hide your malice from men, yet on the day of judgment it will be brought out into the open. Hence it is written in Wisdom: [[Wis 16:15|it is impossible to escape thy hand|Manum tuam, Domine, impossibile est effugere]], O Lord; and in the Psalm: [[Ps 138:7|Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy face|Quo ibo a spiritu tuo, et quo a facie tua fugiam]]? [[3:8|Bring forth therefore fruit worthy of penance|Facite ergo fructum dignum pœnitentiæ]], that is, from the depth of the heart, with a careful watch over the mind and a fearful spirit, lest you fall back. For [[Heb 10:31|it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God|Horrendum est enim incidere in manus Dei viventis]]. That this is the sense seems to follow from what is found further on: when Christ asked the Pharisees, [[Matt 21:25|The baptism of John|Baptismus Joannis]], was it [[Matt 21:25|from heaven or from men|de cœlo erat, an ex hominibus]]?, they did not dare to answer [[Matt 21:26|from heaven|De cœlo]], knowing that He would say to them: [[Matt 21:26|Why then did you not believe him|Quare ergo vos non credidistis ei]]?

paras.t: Quod autem prior expositio aptior sit, apparet ex hoc quod in Luca fertur Christum verba ista dixisse ad turbas communiter. Turbæ autem credebant Joanni: propter quod Pharisæi dicere non audebant, Ex hominibus, propter populum. Omnes enim habebant Joannem quasi prophetam, ut Evangelista disseruit. Probabilius ergo apparet Joannem dixisse hæc verba ad omnes communiter, quorum aliqui boni, aliqui mali fuerunt: non tamen secundum eumdem sensum, nec propter finem eumdem. Nec hoc mirum putetur, quum secundum Augustinum, eadem scriptura habeat sensum litteralem multiplicem. Bonis ergo et pœnitentibus, sed nondum perfectis, sic fatur, ut eos magis humiliet, ad melioraque provocet: frequenter enim viri sancti dure loquuntur etiam valde bonis, propter hanc aut similem causam. Malis vero sic loquitur, ut terreantur atque pœniteant.
paras.en: That the former exposition is the more fitting, however, appears from this, that in Luke we are told that Christ [so the printed text; in Luke iii, 7 it is John who speaks] said these words to the crowds in general. Now the crowds believed John; and that is why the Pharisees did not dare to say [[Matt 21:26|from men|Ex hominibus]], for fear of the people; [[Matt 21:26|for all held John as a prophet|Omnes enim habebant Joannem quasi prophetam]], as the Evangelist has related. It seems more probable, then, that John said these words to all in common, some of whom were good and some wicked, yet not in the same sense nor for the same end. Nor should this be thought strange, since according to Augustine the same scripture may have more than one literal sense. To the good and penitent, then, who were not yet perfect, he speaks thus in order to humble them the more and to stir them to better things; for holy men often speak harshly even to the very good, for this or a like reason. But to the wicked he speaks thus so that they may be terrified and repent.

paras.t: Secundum Chrysostomum, Judæi a Joanne dicuntur progenies viperarum, propter tres viperæ proprietates. Prima est: quum vipera momorderit hominem, statim ipsa currit ad aquam, quam si invenire non potest, mox moritur: sic Judæi peccata mortifera committentes, ad baptismum currebant, ut more viperarum, periculum mortis evaderent. Secunda, nam sicut natura viperarum est rumpere viscera materna et sic nasci, sic Judæi persequentes assidue sanctos Prophetas, corruperunt matrem suam, videlicet Synagogam. Tertia, nam viperæ foris speciosæ et quasi pictæ videntur, intus vero replentur veneno: sic Pharisæi et Sadducæi sanctitatem forinsecus simulabant, sed venenum malitiæ portabant in corde.
paras.en: According to Chrysostom, the Jews are called by John a [[3:7|brood of vipers|progenies viperarum]] because of three properties of the viper. The first is this: when a viper has bitten a man, it at once runs to water, and if it cannot find any, it soon dies; so the Jews, having committed deadly sins, were running to baptism, that after the manner of vipers they might escape the danger of death. The second: as it is the nature of vipers to burst their mother’s womb and so to be born, so the Jews, by constantly persecuting the holy Prophets, destroyed their mother, namely the Synagogue. The third: vipers look comely outwardly and as it were painted, but within they are full of venom; so the Pharisees and Sadducees made an outward show of holiness, but carried the venom of malice in their hearts.

paras.t: Et ne velitis dicere intra vos, id est ne cogitetis inaniter gloriando de ingenitæ carnalis propagationis nobilitate: Patrem habemus Abraham magnum patriarcham, de cujus semine sumus exorti, quasi hoc vobis ad salutem sufficiat. Jactabant etenim se Judæi de dignitate prosapiæ: quod frivolum est, quoniam imitatores fidei atque justitiæ Patriarcharum, potius appellantur filii eorum, quam filii solum carnales. Propter quod Salvator ait Judæis: Si filii Abrahæ estis, opera Abrahæ facite. Quod quoniam non fecerunt, audierunt a Veritate: Vos ex patre diabolo estis. Unde ad Galatas dicit Apostolus: Qui ex fide sunt, hi sunt filii Abrahæ.
paras.en: [[3:9|And think not to say within yourselves|Et ne velitis dicere intra vos]], that is, do not think, glorying vainly in the nobility of your inborn descent according to the flesh: [[3:9|We have Abraham for our father|Patrem habemus Abraham]], the great patriarch, from whose seed we are sprung, as though this were enough for your salvation. For the Jews boasted of the dignity of their lineage; which is a trifling thing, since those who imitate the faith and justice of the Patriarchs are more truly called their children than those who are their children only according to the flesh. For this reason the Saviour says to the Jews: [[John 8:39|If you be the children of Abraham, do the works of Abraham|Si filii Abrahæ estis, opera Abrahæ facite]]. And because they did not do them, they heard from the Truth: [[John 8:44|You are of your father the devil|Vos ex patre diabolo estis]]. Hence the Apostle says to the Galatians: [[Gal 3:7|they who are of faith, the same are the children of Abraham|Qui ex fide sunt, hi sunt filii Abrahæ]].

paras.t: Merito denique non debetis de ista paternitate præsumere, dico enim vobis, quoniam potens est Deus de lapidibus istis suscitare filios Abrahæ: secundum duplicem intellectum. Primo, nam Deus omnipotens, qui cuncta creavit, potest facillime de saxis procreare homines justos, qui sint spirituales filii Abrahæ veriores, nobilioresque filii ejus, quam estis vos. Secundo, quia de gentilibus, qui propter cordis sui duritiam, stoliditatem, ac idololatriam, lapides nominantur, potest misericordia Dei facere homines sanctos et spirituales, qui digni sint dici filii Abrahæ: quemadmodum per Ezechielem affirmat, Auferam cor lapideum de carne vestra, et dabo vobis cor carneum: quod de Judæis litteraliter dicitur. Hanc suscitationem Deus implevit, quando ad prædicationem Apostolorum obstinati sunt Judæi, et gentiles illuminati: quando Deus vocavit non dilectam, dilectam, et non misericordiam consecutam, misericordiam consecutam, sicut Osee prædixit: hoc est, plebem gentilem, quæ tempore suæ perfidiæ fuit non dilecta, et Deo odiosa secundum præsentem justitiam, fecit sibi dilectam, convertendo eam ad fidem. Tunc quoque impletum est illud Isaiæ: Quia multi filii desertæ, id est gentilitatis olim relictæ, magis quam ejus quæ habet virum, hoc est Synagogæ, cujus sponsus et vir exstitit Deus.
paras.en: And rightly you ought not to presume on this fatherhood, [[3:9|For I tell you that God is able of these stones to raise up children to Abraham|dico enim vobis, quoniam potens est Deus de lapidibus istis suscitare filios Abrahæ]]; and this in a twofold sense. First, because almighty God, who created all things, can most easily bring forth from stones just men, who would be truer spiritual children of Abraham, and nobler children of his, than you are. Secondly, because out of the gentiles, who for the hardness, dullness and idolatry of their hearts are called stones, the mercy of God can make holy and spiritual men, worthy to be called children of Abraham; as He declares through Ezechiel: [[Ezech 36:26|I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and will give you a heart of flesh|Auferam cor lapideum de carne vestra, et dabo vobis cor carneum]], which is said of the Jews in the literal sense. God fulfilled this raising up when, at the preaching of the Apostles, the Jews were hardened and the gentiles enlightened; when God called [[Rom 9:25|her that was not beloved, beloved; and her that had not obtained mercy; one that hath obtained mercy|non dilectam, dilectam, et non misericordiam consecutam, misericordiam consecutam]], as Osee foretold [Denis gives the prophecy in the words in which St Paul cites it]: that is, the gentile people, which in the time of its unbelief was not beloved, and hateful to God as to its present justice, He made beloved to Himself by converting it to the faith. Then too was fulfilled that saying of Isaias: [[Is 54:1|for many are the children of the desolate|Quia multi filii desertæ]], that is, of the gentiles, once forsaken, [[Is 54:1|more than of her that hath a husband|magis quam ejus quæ habet virum]], that is, of the Synagogue, whose bridegroom and husband was God.

paras.t: Deinde subditur ratio cur efficaciter pœnitere oporteat. Jam enim securis ad radicem arboris posita est: id est, de proximo imminet vobis interitus mortis atque æternæ damnationis, nisi pœnitentiam dignam egeritis, sicut arbori propinqua instat ruina, quando securis applicatur radici, ut arborem amputet, funditusque evellat. Loquitur autem metaphorice, ut per securim intelligatur rigor seu ultio divinæ justitiæ, quæ frequenter tollit et damnat impœnitentem repente ac improvise, juxta illud Ecclesiastici: Non tardes converti ad Dominum; subito enim veniet ira illius, et in die vindictæ disperdet te. Arbor vero est genus humanum, seu homo quicumque; radix vero est firmitas vel subsistentia vitæ præsentis. Securis ergo, id est rigor divinæ æquitatis, ad radicem arboris, id est ad subsistentiam vitæ hominis, posita est, ut peccatorem tollat et puniat, quoniam Deus paratus est impium exstirpare, prout in Ecclesiastico habetur: In peccatores respicit ira illius. Et ut in libris Machabæorum legitur: A verbis peccatoris ne timueritis, quoniam gloria ejus stercus et vermis; hodie extollitur, et cras non invenietur. Hinc etiam per Ecclesiasten inducitur: Non sit bonum impio, nec prolongentur dies ejus, sed quasi umbra prætereant. Potest quoque per securim intelligi transitus vitæ præsentis, quæ quanto plus prolongatur, tanto amplius breviatur. Unde Ezechias: Præcisa est, inquit, velut a texente vita mea; dum adhuc ordirer succidit me. Vel: Securis, hoc est comminatio sacræ Scripturæ, ad radicem arboris, hoc est ad intellectum hominis, posita est, ut eum hortetur ac terreat. Deus namque in Scripturis comminatur hominibus, ut corrigant semetipsos. Propter quod per Jeremiam protestatur: Numquid non verba mea sunt quasi ignis, et quasi malleus conterens petram?
paras.en: Then is added the reason why it is necessary to repent in earnest. [[3:10|For now the axe is laid to the root of the|Jam enim securis ad radicem arboris posita est]] tree: that is, the destruction of death and of eternal damnation is close upon you, unless you do worthy penance, just as ruin is near at hand for a tree when the axe is put to its root to cut it down and tear it up altogether. He speaks metaphorically, so that by the axe is understood the rigour or vengeance of divine justice, which often takes away and condemns the impenitent suddenly and unforeseen; according to the words of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 5:8|Delay not to be converted to the Lord|Non tardes converti ad Dominum]]; [[Ecclus 5:9|for his wrath shall come on a sudden|subito enim veniet ira illius]], and in the day of vengeance [[Ecclus 5:9|he will destroy thee|disperdet te]]. The tree is the human race, or any man whatever; the root is the stability or continuance of the present life. [[3:10|The axe|Securis]], then, that is, the rigour of divine equity, [[3:10|is laid to the root of the|ad radicem arboris]] tree, that is, to the continuance of man’s life, to take away the sinner and punish him, since God is ready to root out the wicked; as we have it in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 5:7|his wrath looketh upon sinners|In peccatores respicit ira illius]]. And as we read in the books of the Machabees: [[1 Mach 2:62|fear not the words of a sinful man, for his glory is dung and worms|A verbis peccatoris ne timueritis, quoniam gloria ejus stercus et vermis]]: [[1 Mach 2:63|Today he is lifted up, and tomorrow he shall not be found|hodie extollitur, et cras non invenietur]]. Hence too it is said through Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 8:13|let it not be well with the wicked, neither let his days be prolonged, but as a shadow let them pass away|Non sit bonum impio, nec prolongentur dies ejus, sed quasi umbra prætereant]]. By the axe may also be understood the passing of the present life, which, the more it is lengthened, the more it is shortened. Hence Ezechias says: [[Is 38:12|My life is cut off, as by a weaver: whilst I was yet but beginning, he cut me off|Præcisa est, inquit, velut a texente vita mea; dum adhuc ordirer succidit me]]. Or: [[3:10|the axe|Securis]], that is, the threatening of sacred Scripture, [[3:10|is laid to the root of the|ad radicem arboris]] tree, that is, to the understanding of man, to exhort and to terrify him. For God threatens men in the Scriptures so that they may correct themselves; and for this reason He declares through Jeremias: [[Jer 23:29|Are not my words as a fire|Numquid non verba mea sunt quasi ignis]], [[Jer 23:29|and as a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces|et quasi malleus conterens petram]]?

paras.t: Omnis ergo arbor, id est quilibet homo adultus et compos rationis, quæ non facit fructum bonum, id est actum meritorium interiorem vel exteriorem, imo utrumque, si adsit facultas et tempus debitum, excidetur, id est, ab electis separabitur, et in ignem infernalem mittetur. Talis enim non implet præcepta affirmativa. Nec sufficit declinare a malo, sed oportet insuper bene facere. Omissio ergo interdum est peccatum mortale. Hinc servus inutilis jubetur mitti in tenebras exteriores. Et Christus dicit: Omnem palmitem in me non ferentem fructum, tollet eum Pater. Ex præinductis, patescit veritas justitiæ in Joanne, qui sine personarum acceptione peccatores dire redarguit, neminem palpans, nullique blandiens.
paras.en: [[3:10|Every tree therefore|Omnis ergo arbor]], that is, every man who is grown up and has the use of reason, [[3:10|that doth not yield good fruit|quæ non facit fructum bonum]], that is, a meritorious act, inward or outward, or rather both, if the means and the due time are there, [[3:10|shall be cut down|excidetur]], that is, shall be separated from the elect, [[3:10|and cast into the fire|et in ignem infernalem mittetur]] of hell. For such a man does not fulfil the affirmative precepts [the commandments that bid us do something, as distinct from those that forbid]. Nor is it enough to turn away from evil; one must also do good. An omission, therefore, is sometimes a mortal sin. Hence the unprofitable servant is ordered to be cast into the exterior darkness. And Christ says: [[John 15:2|Every branch in me that beareth not fruit, he will take away|Omnem palmitem in me non ferentem fructum, tollet eum]], namely the Father. From what has been said, the truth of John’s justice is plain: without respect of persons he sternly rebuked sinners, coaxing no one and flattering none.

paras.t: Consequenter Joannes ostendit insufficientiam sui baptismi, et propriæ personæ conditionem. Cujus ratio est, ut tangitur in Luca, quoniam omnes opinabantur Joannem esse Christum. Ego quidem baptizo vos in aqua: hoc est, exterius lavo vos aquam super vos fundens; non interius purgo, peccata tollens, aut gratiam conferens. Baptizo ergo et corpora vestra in aqua lavo, in pœnitentiam, id est, ad hoc ut ad pœnitendum vos inducam, non ut peccata dimittam. Qui autem post me venturus est in publicum, id est Christus, qui cito post hæc manifestabit se ipsum, prædicando, miracula faciendo, atque per discipulos suos baptizando, fortior, id est major et dignior, me est, secundum utramque suam naturam: quia ut Deus, est infinitæ potentiæ, dignitatis, ac perfectionis; secundum humanitatem quoque assumptam, data est sibi omnis potestas in cœlo et terra. Pater enim diligit Filium, et omnia dedit in manu ejus: imo Christus ut homo excedit perfectionem, dignitatem et gratiam omnium creaturarum simul sumptarum, propter immediatam et hypostaticam seu personalem unionem suæ humanitatis cum Verbo.
paras.en: Next John shows the insufficiency of his baptism, and the condition of his own person. The reason for this, as is touched on in Luke, is that all thought John was the Christ. [[3:11|I indeed baptize you in water|Ego quidem baptizo vos in aqua]]: that is, I wash you outwardly, pouring water upon you; I do not cleanse you inwardly by taking away sins or conferring grace. I baptize you, then, and wash your bodies in water, [[3:11|unto penance|in pœnitentiam]], that is, to this end, that I may lead you to do penance, not that I may forgive sins. [[3:11|but he that shall come after me|Qui autem post me venturus est]] into public view, that is, Christ, who shortly after this will make Himself known by preaching, by working miracles, and by baptizing through His disciples, [[3:11|is mightier than I|fortior ... me est]], that is, greater and more worthy, according to both His natures: for as God He is of infinite power, dignity and perfection; and according to the humanity He assumed, too, [[Matt 28:18|all power is given|data est ... omnis potestas]] to Him [[Matt 28:18|in heaven and in earth|in cœlo et terra]]. For [[John 3:35|The Father loveth the Son: and he hath given all things into his hand|Pater enim diligit Filium, et omnia dedit in manu ejus]]. Indeed, Christ as man surpasses the perfection, dignity and grace of all creatures taken together, because of the immediate and hypostatic or personal union of His humanity with the Word.

paras.t: Cujus non sum dignus calceamenta portare, hoc est, in tantum excedit me, quod non sum dignus ei in minimo ministrare. De Christo legitur, quod cœpit facere et docere. Quum ergo ipse discipulos suos ad prædicandum miserit sine calceamentis, credibile est quod ipse calceamentis usus non sit. Quod ergo ait Joannes de Christo, Cujus non sum dignus calceamenta portare, intelligendum est secundum communem modum loquendi, quo aliquis volens se multum humiliare sub aliquo, dicit se non esse dignum gerere calceos ejus. Per quod Joannes declarat se incomparabiliter Christo minorem. O quanta humilitas in corde Baptistæ! Merito utique a Christo excellentissime laudari sublimarique meruit, qui se tantum sub illo dejecit, quamvis nec plene se humiliare potuerit per comparationem ad Christum, qui tamen de Joanne testatur: Inter natos mulierum non surrexit major Joanne Baptista.
paras.en: [[3:11|whose shoes I am not worthy to bear|Cujus non sum dignus calceamenta portare]]: that is, He so far surpasses me that I am not worthy to serve Him in the least thing. We read of Christ that He [[Acts 1:1|began to do and to teach|cœpit facere et docere]]. Since, then, He sent His disciples out to preach without shoes, it is credible that He Himself did not wear shoes. What John says of Christ, therefore, [[3:11|whose shoes I am not worthy to bear|Cujus non sum dignus calceamenta portare]], is to be understood according to the common manner of speaking, by which someone who wishes to humble himself greatly beneath another says that he is not worthy to carry his shoes. By this John declares himself to be beyond all comparison less than Christ. O how great was the humility in the Baptist’s heart! Rightly indeed did he deserve to be praised and exalted by Christ most excellently, since he cast himself down so low beneath Him, though he could not humble himself fully in comparison with Christ; and Christ for His part testifies of John: [[Matt 11:11|there hath not risen among them that are born of women a greater than John the Baptist|Inter natos mulierum non surrexit major Joanne Baptista]].

paras.t: Sed quæritur, quum secundum doctores quosdam, homo de condigno possit mereri vitam æternam, quomodo Joannes dignus non fuit Christo in minimo ministrare, seu ejus calceamenta portare. Denique, si dignus fuit et meruit Christum baptizare, quomodo dignus non fuit ei in minimo deservire? Respondendum, quod aliquis dicitur dignus per comparationem ad Christum dupliciter: primo, simpliciter; secundo, secundum modum humanæ possibilitatis et conditionis. Primo modo, nemo dignus fuit, vel est, Christo appropinquare, aut ministrare, propter infinitum excessum suæ perfectionis præ omnibus; tamen secundo modo est aliquis dignus ei servire, imo et corpus et sanguinem ejus consecrare ac manducare, præsertim quum dicat Apostolus: Quicumque manducaverit panem hunc, vel biberit calicem Domini indigne, reus erit corporis et sanguinis Domini.
paras.en: But it is asked: since, according to certain doctors, a man can merit eternal life de condigno [that is, in strict justice, as opposed to merit de congruo, by fittingness], how was John not worthy to serve Christ in the least thing, or to carry His shoes? Again, if he was worthy and merited to baptize Christ, how was he not worthy to serve Him in the least thing? The answer is that a person is called worthy in comparison with Christ in two ways: first, absolutely; secondly, according to the measure of human capacity and condition. In the first way no one was or is worthy to approach Christ or to serve Him, because of the infinite excess of His perfection above all; yet in the second way a person is worthy to serve Him, and even to consecrate and to eat His body and blood, especially since the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 11:27|whosoever shall eat this bread, or drink the chalice of the Lord unworthily, shall be guilty of the body and of the blood of the Lord|Quicumque manducaverit panem hunc, vel biberit calicem Domini indigne, reus erit corporis et sanguinis Domini]].

paras.t: Ipse vos, id est vos ipsos, vel alios per vos designatos et vobis in specie similes, baptizabit per suos ministros, ita quod ipse erit principalis baptizator, mundans interius, ministri vero ipsius erunt baptizatores instrumentales: Christus quippe per se ipsum non baptizavit, ut dicit Joannes; in Spiritu Sancto, id est virtute et gratia Spiritus Sancti, videlicet gratiam Spiritus Sancti infundendo, et vitia diluendo, et igni. Si dixisset, In Spiritu Sancto et aqua, consonare videretur Salvatori dicenti: Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua et Spiritu Sancto, etc. Quid ergo per ignem intelligitur? Puto quod caritatis fervor, de quo Christus dicit: Ignem veni mittere in terram, et quid volo nisi ut accendatur? Christi namque Baptismus ordinatur ad divinæ caritatis perfectionem atque fervorem: propter quod lex evangelica appellatur lex amoris et gratiæ. Baptizabit ergo vos in Spiritu Sancto et igni, id est, baptizando caritatem in vobis accendet, inducendo vos in memoriam beneficiorum suorum. Hieronymus per Spiritum Sanctum et ignem idem intelligit, eo quod Spiritus Sanctus sit ignis, juxta illud Apostoli ad Hebræos: Deus noster ignis consumens est. Sicque conjunctio, Et, tenetur expositive. Chrysostomus et Beda per ignem intelligunt tribulationis atque tentationis fervorem, quo Christifideles purgantur. Nam omnes qui volunt pie vivere in Christo, persecutionem patientur. Lyra per ignem intelligit sensibile signum, in quo Spiritus Sanctus frequenter in primitiva Ecclesia dabatur baptizatis, quemadmodum et Apostolis in die Pentecostes in igneis linguis legitur datus. Alii per ignem intelligunt purgatorii pœnam, in quo post vitam præsentem lavantur atque purgantur qui cum reatu decedunt.
paras.en: [[3:11|he shall baptize you|Ipse vos ... baptizabit]], that is, you yourselves, or others signified by you and like you in kind, through His ministers, in such a way that He will be the principal baptizer, cleansing inwardly, while His ministers will be instrumental baptizers; for Christ did not baptize in His own person, as John says; [[3:11|in the Holy Ghost|in Spiritu Sancto]], that is, by the power and grace of the Holy Ghost, namely by pouring in the grace of the Holy Ghost and washing away sins, [[3:11|and fire|et igni]]. Had he said “in the Holy Ghost and water”, he would seem to agree with the Saviour, who says: [[John 3:5|unless a man be born again of water and the Holy Ghost|Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua et Spiritu Sancto]], etc. What, then, is understood by fire? I think it is the fervour of charity, of which Christ says: [[Luke 12:49|I am come to cast fire on the earth. And what will I, but that it be kindled|Ignem veni mittere in terram, et quid volo nisi ut accendatur]]? For the Baptism of Christ is ordered to the perfection and fervour of divine charity; for which reason the law of the Gospel is called the law of love and of grace. [[3:11|he shall baptize you in the Holy Ghost and fire|Baptizabit ergo vos in Spiritu Sancto et igni]], then, that is, by baptizing He will kindle charity in you, by leading you to remember His benefits. Jerome understands the same thing by the Holy Ghost and by fire, because the Holy Ghost is fire, according to the words of the Apostle to the Hebrews: [[Heb 12:29|our God is a consuming fire|Deus noster ignis consumens est]]. And so the conjunction “and” is taken as explanatory [that is, “in the Holy Ghost, that is to say, in fire”]. Chrysostom and Bede understand by fire the heat of tribulation and temptation, by which the faithful of Christ are purified; for [[2 Tim 3:12|all that will live godly in Christ|omnes qui volunt pie vivere in Christo]] [[2 Tim 3:12|shall suffer persecution|persecutionem patientur]]. Lyra understands by fire the sensible sign in which the Holy Ghost was often given to the baptized in the early Church, as we read that He was given to the Apostles too on the day of Pentecost in fiery tongues. Others understand by fire the pain of purgatory, in which, after the present life, those are washed and cleansed who depart with a debt of punishment still owing [reatus: guilt as liability to punishment].

paras.t: Cujus ventilabrum in manu sua, etc. Ventilabrum est instrumentum quo blada purgantur, separando ea a paleis: per quod intelligitur justum judicium Christi, quo electi a reprobis segregantur. Area autem vocatur Ecclesia, in qua boni ac mali commixti sunt, sicut in area triticum paleaque simul ponuntur. Triticum vero electos significat; horreum vero, regnum cœleste; palea, reprobos. Est igitur sensus: Cujus, videlicet Christi, ventilabrum, id est justum judicium, judiciariaque potestas, est in manu, id est in potestate sua. Pater enim omne judicium dedit Filio, et potestatem dedit ei judicium facere, quia Filius hominis est. Et permundabit, id est, perfecte purgabit, aream suam, id est Ecclesiam militantem, in die judicii, quando separabit agnos ab hædis. Nunc enim perversi cum bonis miscentur, sed tunc loco et præmio separabuntur. Quotidie quoque purgat Deus aream suam dupliciter: primo, impios de hac vita tollendo, ne inficiant simplices; secundo, electos multipliciter castigando, spiritualiter circumcidendo, ad futuram beatitudinem disponendo per tribulationes diversas, quemadmodum in Sapientia scribitur: Tanquam aurum in fornace probavit illos, et quasi holocausti hostiam accepit eos. Reprobos vero dimittit secundum desideria cordis eorum, ut eant in adinventionibus suis: super quos non est virga Dei, ut in Job legitur.
paras.en: [[3:12|Whose fan is in his hand|Cujus ventilabrum in manu sua]], etc. The fan [ventilabrum, the winnowing-fan] is the instrument by which corn is cleaned, by separating it from the chaff; by it is understood the just judgment of Christ, by which the elect are set apart from the reprobate. The floor is the Church, in which good and bad are mingled together, as wheat and chaff lie together on the threshing-floor. The wheat signifies the elect; the barn, the heavenly kingdom; the chaff, the reprobate. The sense, then, is this: [[3:12|Whose|Cujus]], namely Christ’s, [[3:12|fan|ventilabrum]], that is, just judgment and judicial power, [[3:12|is in his hand|in manu]], that is, in His power. For the Father [[John 5:22|hath given all judgment to the Son|omne judicium dedit Filio]], [[John 5:27|And he hath given him power to do judgment, because he is the Son of man|et potestatem dedit ei judicium facere, quia Filius hominis est]]. [[3:12|and he will thoroughly cleanse|Et permundabit]], that is, will cleanse perfectly, [[3:12|his floor|aream suam]], that is, the Church militant, on the day of judgment, when He will separate the lambs from the goats. For now the wicked are mingled with the good, but then they will be separated in place and in reward. Every day, too, God cleanses His floor in two ways: first, by taking the wicked out of this life, so that they may not infect the simple; secondly, by chastising the elect in many ways, circumcising them spiritually, and disposing them for the beatitude to come by various tribulations; as it is written in Wisdom: [[Wis 3:6|As gold in the furnace, he hath proved them, and as a victim of a holocaust, he hath received them|Tanquam aurum in fornace probavit illos, et quasi holocausti hostiam accepit eos]]. But the reprobate He lets go [[Ps 80:13|according to the desires of their heart|secundum desideria cordis eorum]], to walk [[Ps 80:13|in their own inventions|in adinventionibus suis]]; upon such [[Job 21:9|the rod of God is not|non est virga Dei]], as we read in Job.

paras.t: Et congregabit triticum suum in horreum suum, id est electos in regnum supernum, quando dicturus est eis: Venite, benedicti Patris mei, percipite regnum vobis ab origine mundi paratum. Paleas autem, id est infructuosos, leves et reprobos, de quibus in Psalmo: Non sic impii, sed tanquam pulvis quem projicit ventus a facie terræ; comburet, hoc est, puniet, non consumet, igni inexstinguibili, id est flamma et pœna infernali nunquam cessante. Per quod damnatur error dicentium pœnas inferni tandem post longa spatia terminari. Unde in Ezechiele testatur ad impios: Conflabo et congregabo vos, et succendam vos in igne furoris mei, et conflabimini in medio ejus, sicut conflatur argentum in medio ignis. Unde Psalmographus: Cadent, inquit, super eos carbones, in ignem dejicies eos, in miseriis non subsistent. Et Joannes in Apocalypsi: Pars illorum erit in stagno ardenti igne et sulfure, et fumus tormentorum ascendet in sæcula sæculorum. O utinam verba ista terrifica anima sapienter saperet, et aure cordis ea perciperet! Utique nil carnale aut transitorium eam delectaret, sed cum sancto Job diceret: Semper quasi tumentes super me fluctus timui Deum. Sed quum de impiis dicatur, Ad nimium calorem transeant ab aquis nivium: cur de solo igne nunc fit mentio? Dicendum, quod nomine ignis, qualibet gravis afflictio designatur; vel de igne solum fit mentio, tanquam principali tormento.
paras.en: [[3:12|and gather his wheat into the barn|Et congregabit triticum suum in horreum suum]], that is, the elect into the kingdom on high, when He shall say to them: [[Matt 25:34|Come, ye blessed of my Father|Venite, benedicti Patris mei]], receive [[Matt 25:34|the kingdom prepared for you|regnum vobis ab origine mundi paratum]] from the beginning of the world. [[3:12|but the chaff|Paleas autem]], that is, the fruitless, the light and the reprobate, of whom it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 1:4|Not so the wicked|Non sic impii]], [[Ps 1:4|but like the dust, which the wind driveth from the face of the earth|sed tanquam pulvis quem projicit ventus a facie terræ]]; [[3:12|he will burn|comburet]], that is, will punish, not consume, [[3:12|with unquenchable fire|igni inexstinguibili]], that is, with the flame and pain of hell that never ceases. By this is condemned the error of those who say that the pains of hell will at last come to an end after long ages. Hence in Ezechiel He declares to the wicked: I will melt you, and [[Ezech 22:21|will gather you together, and will burn you in the fire of my wrath, and you shall be melted in the midst thereof|congregabo vos, et succendam vos in igne furoris mei, et conflabimini in medio ejus]], [[Ezech 22:22|as silver is melted in the midst|sicut conflatur argentum in medio]] of the fire. Hence the Psalmist says: [[Ps 139:11|Burning coals shall fall upon them; thou wilt cast them down into the fire: in miseries they shall not be able to stand|Cadent, inquit, super eos carbones, in ignem dejicies eos, in miseriis non subsistent]]. And John in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 21:8|they shall have their portion in the pool burning with fire and brimstone|Pars illorum erit in stagno ardenti igne et sulfure]], [[Apoc 14:11|and the smoke of their torments, shall ascend up for ever and ever|et fumus tormentorum ascendet in sæcula sæculorum]]. O that the soul would wisely savour these terrible words, and take them in with the ear of the heart! Then surely nothing carnal or passing would delight it, but it would say with holy Job: [[Job 31:23|I have always feared God as waves swelling over me|Semper quasi tumentes super me fluctus timui Deum]]. But since it is said of the wicked, [[Job 24:19|to excessive heat|Ad nimium calorem]] let them pass [[Job 24:19|from the snow waters|ab aquis nivium]], why is fire alone mentioned here? The answer is that by the name of fire any grievous affliction is signified; or else fire alone is mentioned as the chief torment.

paras.t: Tunc, videlicet Joanne prædicante ac baptizante, venit Jesus a Galilæa, puta a civitate Nazareth, in qua ipse hucusque juvenis habitavit cum Virgine matre, Sponsus cum sponsa, Creator cum creatura, Christus salvator cum Maria prælecta incomparabiliter benedicta: cum qua Deus tanto tempore in terris conversari ac demorari elegit, quia deliciæ ejus esse cum illa. In Jordanem, id est ad loca juxta Jordanis fluenta, ad Joannem Baptistam ut baptizaretur ab eo in Jordane. Cur Agnus sine macula, cur Deus et homo inter populares advenit, vestimenta deposuit, et ut baptizaretur manibus servi se nudum supposuit? O stupendum ac metuendum, pariterque amandum spectaculum! Quid mirum, si expavit Joannes oculis corporalibus hoc cernens, quum et nos sola consideratione intellectualis oculi contremiscamus? Cur ergo hoc factum sit, statim dicetur.
paras.en: [[3:13|Then|Tunc]], that is, while John was preaching and baptizing, [[3:13|cometh Jesus from Galilee|venit Jesus a Galilæa]], namely from the town of Nazareth, in which He had lived until then as a young man with the Virgin His mother: the Bridegroom with the bride, the Creator with the creature, Christ the Saviour with Mary, chosen beforehand and blessed beyond compare; with whom God chose to dwell and abide on earth for so long a time, because His delights were to be with her [an echo of Prov. viii, 31, “my delights were to be with the children of men”]. [[3:13|to the Jordan|In Jordanem]], that is, to the places beside the waters of the Jordan, [[3:13|unto John|ad Joannem]] the Baptist, [[3:13|to be baptized by him|ut baptizaretur ab eo]] in the Jordan. Why did the Lamb without spot, why did God and man come among the common people, lay aside His garments, and put Himself naked beneath the hands of a servant to be baptized? O sight to astonish, to fear, and no less to love! What wonder if John was struck with dread as he beheld this with his bodily eyes, when we too tremble at the mere consideration of it with the eye of the mind? Why this was done will be told presently.

paras.t: Joannes autem ex humilitate prohibebat eum, non per modum imperii, quum hoc sit superioris, sed per modum humillimæ abnegationis, sciens se indignum ad baptizandum Filium Dei: quemadmodum etiam Petrus ait ad Jesum, Non lavabis mihi pedes in æternum. Considerans namque Joannes suam parvitatem, et Christi majestatem, incredibiliter mirabatur de tanta dignatione et humiliatione Dei incarnati. Prohibebat itaque eum publice coram populo, dicens: Ego a te debeo, id est, indigeo, et debito condecentiæ teneor, baptizari Baptismo tuo evangelicæ legis sacramento, vel saltem interiori baptismo: quod et factum est, sicut ait Chrysostomus quod Christus postea baptizavit Joannem. Debuit autem Joannes baptizari a Christo, propter venialium remissionem, propter gratiæ incrementum, propter propriæ doctrinæ approbationem, quatenus ipse faceret ad quod alios hortabatur: admonuit enim alios ut Christi Baptismum susciperent. Apostolos quoque baptizatos esse a Christo probabile est. Et tu venis ad me servum tuum? quasi dicat: Hoc omnino mirabile est, mysteriumque ignoro. Respondens autem Jesus Joanni, dixit ei: Sine, id est, ab hac tua prohibitione cessa, et dimitte me baptizari, modo, id est nunc quum tempus est humiliationis; sic enim, videlicet, ut ego baptizer a te, tuque baptizes me, decet nos ambos, et me specialiter, implere omnem justitiam, id est omnem perfectionem, virtutem, et maxime humilitatem. Hæc est præcipua ratio baptizationis Christi, ut omnem impleret justitiam. Sumitur vero justitia hoc loco communiter, prout omnem virtutem includit. Justum itaque fuit Christum baptizari: Primo, quoniam in hoc natus est, et ad hoc venit in mundum, ut humanam operaretur salutem. Quemadmodum ergo occisus est, ut nos a morte eriperet; sic baptizatus est, ut suo Baptismo animas nostras purgaret, tactuque sui sanctissimi corporis, aquis vim regenerativam præstaret... Tertio, ut baptismum Joannis approbaret. Quarto, ut nobis perfectæ humilitatis formam ostenderet. Quinto, ut primo faceret quod statim edocuit. Docuit enim Christus alios ut baptizarentur. Tunc dimisit eum Joannes, id est, ratione tanti mysterii cognita, dimisit Christum suis se subdere manibus, præparans se ad baptizandum Dominum universorum.
paras.en: [[3:14|But John|Joannes autem]], out of humility, [[3:14|stayed him|prohibebat eum]]: not by way of command, since that belongs to a superior, but by way of a most humble refusal, knowing himself unworthy to baptize the Son of God; just as Peter also said to Jesus: [[John 13:8|Thou shalt never wash my feet|Non lavabis mihi pedes in æternum]]. For John, considering his own littleness and the majesty of Christ, marvelled beyond belief at so great a condescension and humbling of God incarnate. And so he stayed Him publicly before the people, [[3:14|saying: I ought|dicens: Ego a te debeo]], that is, I need, and am bound by a debt of fittingness, [[3:14|to be baptized by thee|baptizari]] with Thy Baptism, the sacrament of the law of the Gospel, or at least with an inward baptism; and this was in fact done, for Chrysostom says that Christ afterwards baptized John. John ought to have been baptized by Christ for the remission of venial sins, for the increase of grace, and for the approval of his own teaching, so that he himself might do what he exhorted others to do; for he urged others to receive the Baptism of Christ. It is probable too that the Apostles were baptized by Christ. [[3:14|and comest thou to me|Et tu venis ad me]], Thy servant? As if to say: This is altogether wonderful, and I do not understand the mystery. [[3:15|And Jesus answering, said to him|Respondens autem Jesus Joanni, dixit ei]]: [[3:15|Suffer it to be so|Sine]], that is, cease from this hindering of thine and let Me be baptized, [[3:15|now|modo]], that is, at present, since it is the time of humiliation; [[3:15|for so|sic enim]], namely, that I be baptized by thee and that thou baptize Me, [[3:15|it becometh us|decet nos]] both, and Me especially, [[3:15|to fulfil all justice|implere omnem justitiam]], that is, all perfection and virtue, and above all humility. This is the chief reason for the baptizing of Christ: that He might fulfil all justice. Justice is taken here in the general sense, as it includes every virtue. It was just, then, that Christ should be baptized: first, because He was born for this, and came into the world for this, to work the salvation of mankind. As, then, He was slain to snatch us from death, so He was baptized that by His Baptism He might cleanse our souls, and by the touch of His most holy body give the waters their regenerating power... [the printed text has these dots and gives no second reason] Thirdly, to approve the baptism of John. Fourthly, to show us the pattern of perfect humility. Fifthly, to do first what He soon afterwards taught; for Christ taught others to be baptized. [[3:15|Then he suffered him|Tunc dimisit eum]], that is, John, having understood the reason of so great a mystery, allowed Christ to submit Himself to his hands, and prepared himself to baptize the Lord of all things.

paras.t: Baptizatus autem Jesus, confestim ascendit de aqua, id est, Jordanem exivit, stans in ripa vel prope. Et ecce aperti sunt ei cœli, non per divisionem cœlestium corporum, quæ incorruptibilia sunt, sed per effectum quemdam cœlestem cœlitus apparentem. Quum enim Pater et Spiritus Sanctus in cœlo habitare et esse dicantur, tunc cœli asseruntur aperiri, quando per subjectam creaturam apparent hominibus. Juxta quem modum orat Psalmista: Domine, inclina cœlos tuos, et descende; Isaias quoque, Utinam (inquit) dirumperes cœlos, et descenderes. Propter quod dicit Hieronymus: Aperti sunt cœli, non reseratione elementorum. Nomine autem elementorum intelligit etiam orbes cœlestes. Et Chrysostomus: Non rupta est creatura cœlestis. Verumtamen advertendum, quod lux quædam copiosa desuper fusa descendit, et circa Christum apparuit, propter quam videbatur quædam scissio sive apertio esse in cœlo, quemadmodum tempore magnæ fulgurationis. Unde Ezechiel, quum visiones Dei describeret, cœlos affirmat apertos fuisse. Similiter Stephanus de apertione cœlorum loquitur. Sic ergo aperti sunt ei, videlicet Christo, id est ad manifestandam gloriam ejus, cœli omnes. Et vidit visione corporali ipse Christus, sive Joannes: uterque enim eorum vidit quod subditur: Spiritum Dei, id est Spiritum Sanctum, descendentem sicut columbam, id est in forma columbæ, et venientem super se, id est, sedentem super caput Christi, ut supra Apostolos sedit in igneis linguis. Unde Joannes Baptista ait: Vidi Spiritum descendentem de cœlo quasi columbam, et mansit super eum. Hanc columbam angelus ex materia elementari formavit, ut dicitur, eamque movit; sed ipsa Spiritum Sanctum repræsentavit: quæ ministerio suo peracto, in præjacentem est reversa materiam.
paras.en: [[3:16|And Jesus being baptized, forthwith came out of the water|Baptizatus autem Jesus, confestim ascendit de aqua]], that is, He went out of the Jordan, standing on the bank or near it. [[3:16|and lo, the heavens were opened to him|Et ecce aperti sunt ei cœli]], not by a division of the heavenly bodies, which are incorruptible, but by a certain heavenly effect appearing from heaven. For since the Father and the Holy Ghost are said to dwell and to be in heaven, the heavens are said to be opened when they appear to men through some created thing beneath them. In this sense the Psalmist prays: [[Ps 143:5|Lord, bow down thy heavens and descend|Domine, inclina cœlos tuos, et descende]]; and Isaias too: [[Is 64:1|O that thou wouldst rend the heavens, and wouldst come down|Utinam (inquit) dirumperes cœlos, et descenderes]]. For this reason Jerome says: “The heavens were opened, not by an unbarring of the elements”; and by the name of elements he understands the heavenly spheres as well. And Chrysostom: “The heavenly creation was not broken.” Yet it should be noted that an abundant light poured down from above and appeared about Christ, because of which there seemed to be a kind of rending or opening in the sky, as at a time of great lightning. So Ezechiel, when describing the visions of God, declares that the heavens were opened; and Stephen likewise speaks of the opening of the heavens. Thus, then, all [[3:16|the heavens were opened to him|aperti sunt ei ... cœli]], namely to Christ, that is, to make His glory manifest. [[3:16|and he saw|Et vidit]] with bodily sight, Christ Himself, or John; for each of them saw what follows: [[3:16|the Spirit of God|Spiritum Dei]], that is, the Holy Ghost, [[3:16|descending as a dove|descendentem sicut columbam]], that is, in the form of a dove, [[3:16|and coming upon him|et venientem super se]], that is, resting upon the head of Christ, as He rested upon the Apostles in fiery tongues. Hence John the Baptist says: [[John 1:32|I saw the Spirit coming down, as a dove from heaven; and he remained upon him|Vidi Spiritum descendentem de cœlo quasi columbam, et mansit super eum]]. This dove an angel formed from the matter of the elements, as is said, and moved it; but it represented the Holy Ghost; and when its service was done it returned into the matter from which it was made.

paras.t: Et ecce vox de cœlis intonuit, dicens. Vox ista ab angelo formata est in persona Dei Patris, qui dicitur apparuisse in voce, non quia visus, sed quia auditus. Hic est Filius meus naturalis, coæternus et unicus, non adoptivus, dilectus: quem secundum quod Deus est, tantum diligo, sicut me ipsum, videlicet superæstuanti, dulcissimo, penitusque infinito amore; secundum vero humanitatem ejus assumptam, Verbo unitam, diligo eum amplius quam totum universum, quoniam majus bonum contuli ei soli, quam omnibus aliis simul, videlicet personalem unionem cum Verbo, et gratiam sine mensura. In quo mihi complacui, id est, de ipso et ejus perfectione in me ipso complacentiam delectationemque habeo, tanquam qui talem filium genui, tam speciosum, sanctum, et mihi omnino simillimum. Si enim lætatur Deus in operibus suis, et si beneplacitum est Domino in populo suo, quanto magis in Filio suo unigenito delectatur et complacet, in quo nil dissimilitudinis, nil contrarietatis, nil mali invenitur? Denique secundum divinitatem Christi, complacet sibi Pater in Christo, complacentia infinita; secundum humanitatem vero assumptam, habet in eo complacentiam singularem, tanquam in filio obedientissimo. Unde et ita potest exponi: In quo mihi complacui, id est, in quo voluntas mea implebitur, quantum ad reparationem generis humani. Propter quod Christus testatur: Quæ placita sunt ei, facio semper.
paras.en: [[3:17|And behold a voice from heaven|Et ecce vox de cœlis]] thundered, [[3:17|saying|dicens]]. This voice was formed by an angel in the person of God the Father, who is said to have appeared in the voice, not because He was seen, but because He was heard. [[3:17|This is my|Hic est]] [[3:17|Son|Filius meus]], natural, co-eternal and only-begotten, not adopted, [[3:17|beloved|dilectus]]: whom, as He is God, I love as much as Myself, namely with an overflowing, most sweet and wholly infinite love; and according to the humanity He assumed, united to the Word, I love Him more than the whole universe, since I have given to Him alone a greater good than to all others together, namely personal union with the Word, and grace without measure. [[3:17|in whom I am well pleased|In quo mihi complacui]], that is, I have in Myself complacency and delight in Him and in His perfection, as one who has begotten such a Son, so beautiful, so holy, and wholly like to Myself. For if God doth [[Ps 103:31|rejoice in his works|lætatur ... in operibus suis]], and if [[Ps 149:4|the Lord is well pleased with his people|beneplacitum est Domino in populo suo]], how much more does He delight and take pleasure in His only-begotten Son, in whom no unlikeness, no contrariety, no evil is found? According to the divinity of Christ, then, the Father is well pleased in Christ with an infinite complacency; and according to the humanity He assumed, He has in Him a singular complacency, as in a most obedient son. Hence it may also be expounded thus: [[3:17|in whom I am well pleased|In quo mihi complacui]], that is, in whom My will shall be fulfilled as regards the restoring of the human race. For this reason Christ testifies: [[John 8:29|I do always the things that please him|Quæ placita sunt ei, facio semper]].

paras.t: Circa præhabita quæritur, an baptizati baptismo Joannis erant rebaptizandi Baptismate Christi. De hoc duplex fuit opinio: una dicentium, quod quia baptismus Joannis præparatorius fuit ad Christum, idcirco si baptismum illum suscipiens retulit eum ad Christum, constituendo spem suam in gratia ejus, non indiguit denuo baptizari. Hæc est opinio Magistri (libro quarto). Thomas vero et alii multi dicunt, quod quia sacramenta novæ legis gratiam conferunt ex opere operato, idcirco, quando Baptismus Christi fuit de necessitate salutis, non suffecit baptismus Joannis cum relatione prædicta, sed baptizati baptismo Joannis, baptizandi erant Baptismate Christi, sicut et Paulus in Actibus Apostolorum fecisse narratur. Et ista opinio roboratur verbis Augustini, qui dicit super Joannem: Baptizavit Joannes, et baptizatum non est; baptizavit Judas, et baptizatum est.
paras.en: Concerning what has been said, it is asked whether those baptized with the baptism of John had to be baptized again with the Baptism of Christ. On this there were two opinions. One is that of those who say that, since the baptism of John was preparatory to Christ, if one who received that baptism referred it to Christ, placing his hope in His grace, he did not need to be baptized again. This is the opinion of the Master [Peter Lombard, the Master of the Sentences] (in the fourth book). But Thomas and many others say that, since the sacraments of the new law confer grace ex opere operato [by the very performance of the rite], therefore, once the Baptism of Christ had become necessary for salvation, the baptism of John with the reference just mentioned was not enough, but those baptized with the baptism of John had to be baptized with the Baptism of Christ, as Paul too is related to have done in the Acts of the Apostles. And this opinion is strengthened by the words of Augustine, who says on John: “John baptized, and it was not baptism; Judas baptized, and it was baptism.”

paras.t: Insuper quæritur, cur Spiritus Sanctus in forma columbæ apparuit in baptismo. Dicendum, quod per columbam innocentia, puritas, atque simplicitas designantur: quæ omnia ad bonitatem pertinent, quæ Spiritui Sancto appropriatur. Convenienter ergo in specie columbæ ostensus est. Secundo, ad designandum quod in Christo vera innocentia, summa puritas, et circumspecta simplicitas fuit. Tertio, ad denotandum quod per Baptismum homo ad originalem innocentiam, puritatem ac simplicitatem revertitur, dum ab omni labe peccati mundatur, et omni virtute infusa subito decoratur.
paras.en: It is asked further why the Holy Ghost appeared in the form of a dove at the baptism. The answer is that by the dove innocence, purity and simplicity are signified, all of which belong to goodness, which is appropriated to the Holy Ghost [that is, attributed to Him in particular, though it is common to all three Persons]. Fittingly, then, He was shown in the form of a dove. Secondly, to signify that in Christ there was true innocence, the highest purity, and a prudent simplicity. Thirdly, to denote that through Baptism man returns to the original innocence, purity and simplicity, when he is cleansed from every stain of sin and at once adorned with every infused virtue.

paras.t: Quæritur, cur Spiritus Sanctus descendit super Christum baptizatum. Respondendum, quod primo, quatenus Joannes plenius instrueretur de Christo et efficacia sui Baptismatis. Propter quod ait: Ego nesciebam eum; sed qui misit me baptizare in aqua, ille mihi dixit: Super quem videris Spiritum descendentem, hic est qui baptizat in Spiritu Sancto. Secundo, ut Joannes dignitatem et gloriam Christi populo nuntiaret: sicut et fecit, juxta illud: Testimonium perhibuit Joannes, dicens: Quia vidi Spiritum descendentem, et mansit super eum. Rursusque: Ego (inquit) vidi, et testimonium perhibui, quia hic est Filius Dei. Tertio, ad demonstrandum plenitudinem gratiæ Christi, cujus gratia in baptismo aucta non est. Quarto, propter mysterium, scilicet ad insinuandum quod baptizatis Christi Baptismo Spiritus Sanctus infunditur, regnumque cœleste aperitur: ideo enim et cœli aperti sunt. Tunc quoque Trinitas superbenedicta monstrata est, in cujus nomine Christi Baptismus confertur: quæ usque ad illud tempus, nulli præcedentium Patriarcharum aut Prophetarum ita aperte atque distincte revelata est sicut Joanni, in quo ejus excellentia declaratur. Tunc enim Pater apparuit in voce, quæ formata fuit in aere, ad insinuandum quod dicendo, genuit unicum Filium suum, qui est verbum ore Patris æternaliter intellectualiterque prolatum, juxta illud Ecclesiastici: Ego ex ore Altissimi prodivi, primogenita ante omnem creaturam. Filius vero apparuit in humanitate assumpta; Spiritus Sanctus in columba, non utique sicut assumpta, sed velut in signo repræsentativo.
paras.en: It is asked why the Holy Ghost descended upon Christ when He had been baptized. The answer is: first, that John might be more fully instructed about Christ and about the efficacy of His Baptism. For this reason he says: [[John 1:33|I knew him not: but he who sent me to baptize with water said to me: He upon whom thou shalt see the Spirit descending|Ego nesciebam eum; sed qui misit me baptizare in aqua, ille mihi dixit: Super quem videris Spiritum descendentem]], [[John 1:33|he it is that baptizeth with the Holy Ghost|hic est qui baptizat in Spiritu Sancto]]. Secondly, that John might proclaim the dignity and glory of Christ to the people; as he did, according to the words: [[John 1:32|John gave testimony, saying: I saw the Spirit coming down|Testimonium perhibuit Joannes, dicens: Quia vidi Spiritum descendentem]], [[John 1:32|and he remained upon him|et mansit super eum]]. And again he says: [[John 1:34|I saw: and I gave testimony that this is the Son of God|Ego (inquit) vidi, et testimonium perhibui, quia hic est Filius Dei]]. Thirdly, to show the fulness of Christ’s grace, whose grace was not increased at the baptism. Fourthly, for the sake of the mystery, namely to suggest that the Holy Ghost is poured into those baptized with the Baptism of Christ, and the heavenly kingdom is opened to them; for that is why the heavens too were opened. Then also was shown the most blessed Trinity, in whose name the Baptism of Christ is conferred; which until that time had been revealed to none of the Patriarchs or Prophets who went before so openly and distinctly as to John, and in this his excellence is declared. For then the Father appeared in the voice, which was formed in the air, to suggest that by speaking He begot His only Son, who is the Word uttered eternally and intellectually from the mouth of the Father; according to the words of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 24:5|I came out of the mouth of the most High, the firstborn before all creatures|Ego ex ore Altissimi prodivi, primogenita ante omnem creaturam]]. The Son appeared in the humanity He had assumed; the Holy Ghost in the dove, not indeed as assumed, but as in a sign that represented Him.

paras.t: Postremo quæritur, an solus Joannes viderit columbam super Christum descendentem, an etiam ipse audierit solus vocem Patris, præsupposito quod Christus vidit et audivit illam et istam. De hoc nil legi; sed apparet quod sic: aliter non indiguisset [Joannes] testari populo, quemadmodum viderit Spiritum Sanctum in Christum descendere.
paras.en: Lastly, it is asked whether John alone saw the dove descending upon Christ, and whether he alone heard the voice of the Father, it being presupposed that Christ saw the one and heard the other. On this I have read nothing; but it seems that it was so: otherwise John would not have needed to testify to the people how he had seen the Holy Ghost descending upon Christ.

4.title: Elucidatio capituli quarti: Tunc ductus est Jesus in desertum a Spiritu
4.title_en: Explanation of the fourth chapter: “Then Jesus was led by the spirit into the desert”

paras.t: Ostensa vera divinitate humanitateque Christi, consequenter tendit Evangelista ad describendam conversationem ipsius, cujus tota actio nostra instructio est. Tunc, videlicet mox ut baptizatus est, ductus est rationabili suggestione atque interna inspiratione, Jesus in desertum a Spiritu Sancto, qui animam Christi induxit ad hoc ut ingrederetur desertum, propter rationabiles causas. Christus quippe ut homo, plenissimus fuit septem donis Spiritus Sancti, quemadmodum in Isaia legitur: Requiescet super eum Spiritus Domini, etc. Sicut autem virtutes morales efficiunt hominem prompte mobilem a ratione, ut ejus sequatur judicium, sic dona Spiritus Sancti reddunt eum faciliter mobilem a Spiritu Sancto. Idcirco Christus homo a Spiritu Sancto directus, ductus et motus est, ut introiret desertum. Unde Lucas dicit, quod agebatur a Spiritu in desertum. Qui autem Spiritu Dei aguntur, hi sunt filii Dei. Quod enim hoc loco per spiritum designetur Spiritus Sanctus, patet ex duobus: Primo, quoniam in Luca [ubi] dictum est, Jesus plenus Spiritu Sancto regressus est a Jordane; mox subditur, Et agebatur a Spiritu in desertum. Secundo, quia hoc loco, quum dictum est, Ductus est in desertum a Spiritu, subjungitur, Ut tentaretur a diabolo: per quod notatur distinctio inter Spiritum et diabolum. Potest quoque per spiritum quo ductus est Jesus, intelligi spiritus ejus rationalis creatus, videlicet anima (de quo ait: Spiritus quidem promptus est, caro autem infirma), ad denotandum quod propria atque spontanea voluntate, et ex rationis judicio, non coacte, desertum ingressus sit. Dicunt aliqui, quod desertum de quo jam sermo, sit illud quod est inter Jerusalem et Jericho.
paras.en: Having shown the true divinity and humanity of Christ, the Evangelist next proceeds to describe His manner of life, all of whose action is our instruction. [[4:1|Then|Tunc]], that is, as soon as He had been baptized, [[4:1|Jesus was led|ductus est Jesus]], by a reasonable prompting and an inward inspiration, [[4:1|into the desert|in desertum]] [[4:1|by the spirit|a Spiritu]], that is, by the Holy Ghost, who moved the soul of Christ to enter the desert, for reasonable causes. For Christ as man was most full of the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost, as we read in Isaias: [[Is 11:2|And the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him|Requiescet super eum Spiritus Domini]], etc. And just as the moral virtues make a man promptly movable by reason, so that he follows its judgment, so the gifts of the Holy Ghost render him readily movable by the Holy Ghost. Therefore Christ as man, directed by the Holy Ghost, was led and moved to go into the desert. Hence Luke says that He [[Luke 4:1|was led|agebatur]] [[Luke 4:1|by the spirit into the desert|a Spiritu in desertum]]. And [[Rom 8:14|whosoever are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God|Qui autem Spiritu Dei aguntur, hi sunt filii Dei]]. That the Holy Ghost is meant in this place by “the spirit” is plain from two things. First, because in Luke, where it is said, [[Luke 4:1|Jesus being full of the Holy Ghost, returned from the Jordan|Jesus plenus Spiritu Sancto regressus est a Jordane]], there follows at once, [[Luke 4:1|and was led|Et agebatur]] [[Luke 4:1|by the spirit into the desert|a Spiritu in desertum]]. Secondly, because in this place, when it has been said, [[4:1|was led by the spirit into the desert|Ductus est in desertum a Spiritu]], there is added, [[4:1|to be tempted by the devil|Ut tentaretur a diabolo]]: by which a distinction is marked between the Spirit and the devil. By the spirit by which Jesus was led may also be understood His own created rational spirit, namely His soul (of which He says: [[Matt 26:41|The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak|Spiritus quidem promptus est, caro autem infirma]]), to denote that He entered the desert of His own free and spontaneous will and by the judgment of reason, not under compulsion. Some say that the desert now spoken of is the one that lies between Jerusalem and Jericho.

paras.t: Oportet advertere, quod multiplex est spiritus, scilicet increatus, qui est incircumscriptus, videlicet Deus, et creatus ac circumscriptus. Spiritus quoque creatus, alius est rationalis, alius irrationalis: de quo Salomon, Quis scit, si spiritus filiorum hominum ascendat, et spiritus jumentorum descendat? Spiritus autem rationalis creatus, alius est conjunctus, ut anima rationalis, alius separatus. Et iste est duplex: alter enim est ad Deum inavertibiliter conversus, ut angelus; alius a Deo inconvertibiliter aversus, ut dæmon.
paras.en: It should be noted that “spirit” is of many kinds: namely uncreated, which is uncircumscribed [that is, not bounded by any place or limit], that is, God; and created and circumscribed. Created spirit, again, is either rational or irrational; of which Solomon says: [[Eccles 3:21|Who knoweth if the spirit of the children of Adam ascend upward, and if the spirit of the beasts descend downward?|Quis scit, si spiritus filiorum hominum ascendat, et spiritus jumentorum descendat?]] [Denis reads “of the children of men”, without “upward” and “downward”.] Created rational spirit, in turn, is either joined to a body, as the rational soul, or separate. And the separate is of two kinds: one turned towards God so that it can never be turned away, as an angel; the other turned away from God so that it can never be converted, as a demon.

paras.t: Denique ratio subditur, cur in desertum ductus est Jesus: Ut tentaretur a diabolo. Ista est una causa, non tamen tota, nec sola, neque præcipua. Poterat namque et extra illud tentari, sicut et in pinnaculo templi tentatus est. Sunt ergo et aliæ causæ potiores. Prima, ut solitariam vitam commendaret, atque eremiticæ ac anachoreticæ conversationis exemplum præberet. Secunda, ut pro nostris peccatis in eremo pœnitentiam, id est opera satisfactoria, ageret. Tertia, ut formam vitandi laudem hominum demonstraret. Mox enim ut a Joanne tam magnifice commendatus est populo, secessit in eremum. Et nos ergo laudati, quæramus abscondi, amantes nesciri. Voluit quoque Christus tentari, ut nos ad tentationes perferendas animaret, ut gratiam triumphandi nobis mereretur, ut formam vincendi ostenderet, ut tentatoris virtutem debilitaret, nosque a tentationibus liberaret. Aliam rationem tangit Apostolus ad Hebræos: Debuit, inquit, per omnia fratribus similari, ut misericors fieret, et fidelis pontifex ad Deum: in quo enim passus est ipse et tentatus, potens est et eis qui tentantur auxiliari.
paras.en: Lastly the reason is added why Jesus was led into the desert: [[4:1|to be tempted by the devil|Ut tentaretur a diabolo]]. This is one cause, yet not the whole, nor the only one, nor the chief. For He could have been tempted outside it as well, just as He was tempted on the pinnacle of the temple. There are therefore other and weightier causes. The first, to commend the solitary life and give an example of the hermit’s and anchorite’s way of life. The second, to do penance in the wilderness for our sins, that is, works of satisfaction. The third, to show the way of avoiding the praise of men: for as soon as He had been so magnificently commended to the people by John, He withdrew into the wilderness. So we too, when we are praised, should seek to be hidden, loving to be unknown. Christ also willed to be tempted in order to encourage us to bear temptations, to merit for us the grace to triumph, to show us the way to conquer, to weaken the power of the tempter, and to set us free from temptations. The Apostle touches on another reason in the Epistle to the Hebrews, where he says: [[Heb 2:17|it behoved him in all things to be made like unto his brethren, that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest before God|Debuit, inquit, per omnia fratribus similari, ut misericors fieret, et fidelis pontifex ad Deum]]: [[Heb 2:18|for in that wherein he himself hath suffered and been tempted he is able to succour them also that are tempted|in quo enim passus est ipse et tentatus, potens est et eis qui tentantur auxiliari]].

paras.t: Et quum jejunasset quadraginta diebus artificialibus, et quadraginta noctibus: non utique eo modo sicut nos jejunamus, qui quotidie semel reficimur, et tamen jejunare censemur; sed tanto tempore nullum corporeum cibum sumpsit, nec potum. Unde in Luca habetur: Nihil manducavit in illis diebus. Postea esuriit, non necessitate naturæ, sed divina dispensatione ac propria voluntate. Quamvis enim omnino supernaturale sit hominem tot diebus nil edere, sicut in Moyse et Elia, tamen in Christo mirabilius fuit quod postea esuriit, quam quod interim nihil comedit: quia ut ait Augustinus in epistola ad Dioscorum, Tanta exstitit beatitudo animæ Christi, quod ex redundantia ejus poterat corpus Christi ab omni passione et læsione præservari, et præservatum fuisset nisi Deo dispensante redundantia illa fuisset suspensa usque ad resurrectionem. Non ergo indiguit cibo, nisi ex voluntate qua voluit redundantiam beatitudinis animæ suæ in corpus suspendi. Esuriit quoque, ut sua fame mereretur nobis gratiam magnam, et animæ saturitatem. Quidquid enim fecit aut pertulit ut viator, nobis meritorium fuit. Item, ut assumptæ humanitatis veritatem ostenderet; rursus, ut dæmoni daret occasionem tentandi. In veteri Testamento leguntur Moyses et Elias tot jejunasse diebus: de quorum esurie nihil subjungitur. Certum est tamen, quod postea esurierunt.
paras.en: [[4:2|And when he had fasted forty days|Et quum jejunasset quadraginta diebus]] — artificial days [that is, days reckoned from sunrise to sunset, as distinct from the natural day of twenty-four hours] — [[4:2|and forty nights|et quadraginta noctibus]]: not, of course, in the way we fast, who take one meal a day and are nonetheless reckoned to be fasting; but for all that time He took no bodily food, nor drink. Hence it is said in Luke: [[Luke 4:2|he ate nothing in those days|Nihil manducavit in illis diebus]]. [[4:2|afterwards he was hungry|Postea esuriit]], not by necessity of nature, but by divine dispensation and His own will. For although it is altogether above nature for a man to eat nothing for so many days, as in Moses and Elias, yet in Christ it was more wonderful that He afterwards hungered than that meanwhile He ate nothing; for, as Augustine says in his letter to Dioscorus, so great was the beatitude of Christ’s soul that by its overflow the body of Christ could have been preserved from all suffering and injury, and would have been preserved, had not that overflow been held back by God’s dispensation until the resurrection. He did not need food, then, except by the will by which He willed the overflow of His soul’s beatitude into His body to be held back. He hungered also that by His hunger He might merit for us great grace and the soul’s fill; for whatever He did or bore as a wayfarer [that is, in the state of this mortal life, as distinct from the blessed in heaven] was meritorious for us. Again, to show the reality of the humanity He had assumed; and again, to give the demon an occasion of tempting. In the Old Testament we read that Moses and Elias fasted for as many days, and nothing is added about their hunger; yet it is certain that they afterwards hungered.

paras.t: Quæritur, quare Salvator non jejunavit diutius quam Moyses et Elias. Dicendum, ne ejus divinitas pateret diabolo. Et etiam propter mysticam rationem, eo quod quadragenarius numerus conveniat pœnitentiæ: constat namque ex denario quater ducto, sicque significat castigationem hominis ex quatuor elementis compositi, cum observatione Decalogi secundum quatuor Evangeliorum doctrinam. Et iterum, quoniam tot diebus jejunando, offerimus Deo decimas anni sive dierum, cui et aliarum rerum decimas offerre jubemur, secundum Gregorium.
paras.en: It is asked why the Saviour did not fast longer than Moses and Elias. The answer is: lest His divinity should become plain to the devil. And also for a mystical reason, because the number forty befits penance: for it is made up of ten taken four times, and so signifies the chastening of man, who is composed of the four elements, together with the keeping of the Decalogue according to the teaching of the four Gospels. And again, because by fasting so many days we offer to God the tithe of the year, or of its days, to whom we are commanded to offer the tithes of other things as well, according to Gregory [who reckons the thirty-six fasting days of Lent, Sundays excepted, as a tithe of the year’s days].

paras.t: Et accedens tentator, dixit ei. Iste tentator et dæmon fertur fuisse Lucifer: quod Magister Sententiarum sentire videtur. Hilarius quoque testatur, quod fuerit dæmonum princeps. Accessit autem ad Christum in forma visibili et humana, et forte in forma hominis religiosi, ut simulata sanctitate circumdatus, citius falleret. Porro tentare proprie sumptum, est experientiam explorare de re ignorata, vel dubia. Dæmon ergo dubitavit de Jesu Nazareno, an esset Christus, idcirco optavit certificari de hoc: habuit namque pro utraque parte rationes sibi quodammodo insolubiles.
